Hierarchical Bayesian models in astronomy

Physics × Machine Learning — Bayesian astrostatistics

Hierarchical Bayesian models
Inferring populations from imperfect data

Astronomy almost never measures a thing directly. It measures many noisy, incomplete, selection-biased proxies and must infer the population behind them: the mass distribution of black holes, the intrinsic scatter of a scaling relation, the abundance of Earth-like planets. Hierarchical Bayesian models (HBMs) are the natural language for this — they model the individual objects and the population that generated them at the same time, propagating every uncertainty coherently.

The structure

Objects have parameters θi; those are drawn from a population governed by hyperparameters φ; the data yi are noisy views of θi. Infer φ and every θi jointly.

Why it wins

It borrows strength across objects (shrinkage), propagates measurement error, and — crucially in astronomy — corrects for selection effects and truncation that bias any naive estimate.

What’s inside

The structure and math; partial pooling, measurement error and selection (with worked figures); the inference machinery (MCMC, the funnel, VI, nested sampling, SBI); model checking; and related techniques.

Where it’s used

Supernova cosmology, the distance ladder, photo-z, gravitational-wave populations, exoplanet occurrence, Gaia distances, galaxy scaling relations — a whole page of examples each.

Tabs above, or Prev / Next (or ← → arrow keys), move through the pages. A companion deck covers Bayesian evidence & model selection.

The anatomy of a hierarchical model

Three layers. Data yi depend on per-object latent parameters θi through a measurement model p(yi|θi). The θi are themselves drawn from a population distribution p(θi|φ) governed by hyperparameters φ, which carry their own hyperprior p(φ). In ‘plate’ shorthand:

φ ~ hyperprior
  └─ for each object i = 1…N:
     θi ~ p(θi | φ)    (population)
     yi ~ p(yi | θi)    (measurement)

The full posterior over everything follows from Bayes’ theorem — and it factorises along the graph:

p(φ, {θi} | {yi})  ∝  p(φ)  ∏i   p(yi | θi)   p(θi | φ) measurement × population × hyperprior — the whole model on one line

The population posterior

Often you care about the population φ, not each θi. Marginalise the latent parameters — each integral is per-object and independent:

p(φ | {yi})  ∝  p(φ)  ∏i ∫ p(yi | θi)   p(θi | φ)   dθi the marginal likelihood of the population — each factor is an ‘evidence’ for object i under φ

This is the engine. Everything else — shrinkage, error propagation, selection corrections — is a consequence of writing down these two lines honestly and doing the integrals.

Interactive: watch the hierarchy generate data

Press Generate to run the model top-down: draw the hyperparameters φ = (μ, τ), then each object’s latent θi from the population, then each noisy datum yi. This is the model as a data generator — inference just runs it backwards.

Top: the population N(μ, τ). Middle: latent θi drawn from it (blue). Bottom: observed yi = θi + noise (dark, with error bars). Watch the generative flow cascade down.
Why ‘exchangeable’ matters. Treating objects as drawn from a common population (de Finetti’s exchangeability) is exactly what licenses the shared prior p(θi|φ) — and what lets one object’s data inform another’s estimate.

Borrowing strength: partial pooling

Two extremes are both wrong. No pooling fits each object alone — noisy and overconfident. Complete pooling forces them all equal — it ignores real differences. The hierarchy interpolates: each estimate is pulled toward the population mean by an amount set by its own noise. For the conjugate Gaussian case the posterior mean is exactly a precision-weighted blend:

θ̂i = (1 − Bi) yi + Bi μ,     Bi = σi2 / (σi2 + τ2) Bi is the shrinkage factor: noisy objects (large σi) are pulled hard toward μ; precise ones barely move

Left: raw estimates (dark) and their hierarchical posterior means (blue) — the noisiest objects shrink most toward the population mean (red). Right: the shrinkage factor Bi vs the measurement error.

This is not an ad-hoc ‘regularisation’: it is the optimal thing to do if the objects really are exchangeable draws from a population, and it provably beats treating each in isolation (the Stein / Efron–Morris result). The population parameters μ, τ are learned from the data themselves — the model decides how much to pool.

Interactive: combine measurements, and tune the pooling

Below, ten ‘experiments’ each measure the same quantity with their own error bar — think of separate measurements of a particle mass or coupling constant (particle physics), or of H0 (cosmology). Drag the population scale τ: at τ→0 they collapse to one complete-pooled world average; at τ→∞ each stands alone (no pooling); in between, each shrinks toward the average by an amount set by its own precision. Add a discrepant measurement to see how a tension is absorbed.

Dark points: raw measurements yi ± σi. Blue: the partially-pooled (shrunk) estimates. Red line: the population mean μ. Noisy measurements shrink most.

This is exactly how particle physics forms world averages (the PDG combination) and how cosmology quantifies the Hubble tension: a hierarchical model asks not just “what is the average?” but “how much do the measurements genuinely disagree?” — the population scale τ is that disagreement.

Read-off. Shrinkage is the visible signature of a hierarchy: individual answers become more accurate because they are estimated together.

Measurement error done right

Every astronomical quantity carries an error bar, and errors in the independent variable are especially treacherous. Fit a scaling relation with ordinary least squares and the slope comes out attenuated — ‘regression dilution’. The hierarchical fix is to treat the true values as latent variables with a population distribution and marginalise them:

p(yiobs, xiobs | φ) = ∫ p(yiobs, xiobs | xi)   p(xi | φ)   dxi integrate over the unknown true xi, given its population — the errors-in-variables / structural model

A linear relation with errors in both axes and intrinsic scatter. Naive OLS returns an attenuated slope (b = 1.29); the hierarchical model recovers the truth (b = 1.40).

Three variances must be kept distinct: the measurement error (known per point), the intrinsic scatter σint (real object-to-object variation about the relation), and the population spread of the covariate. Conflating them is the most common modelling error in astronomy; separating them is exactly what a hierarchy does. This is the content of Kelly (2007), the standard reference for fitting relations with scatter.

Interactive: measurement error and the attenuated slope

Drag the measurement-error slider. As the errors grow, ordinary least squares (gold) flattens — regression dilution — while correcting for the known x-error variance (blue) recovers the true slope (dashed).

Points with x- and y-error bars. Dashed navy: the true relation (b = 1.4). Gold: naive OLS (attenuated). Blue: corrected for the x-error variance.
Latent variables everywhere. Distances, extinctions, true fluxes, redshifts — the quantity you care about is almost always latent behind the data. Model it as such and the uncertainty propagates itself.

The killer app: selection effects

Surveys see the bright, the near, the large. Any sample is truncated by its selection function, and the naive population estimate is biased — the classic Malmquist bias. A hierarchical model handles it exactly, because it knows the data were generated and then selected. The likelihood of the detected sample divides by the probability of detection:

p(data | φ) = ∏i detected   p(yi | φ)  /  Pdet(φ),    Pdet(φ) = ∫ pdet(y) p(y | φ) dy the normalising Pdet — the expected detected fraction — is what corrects the bias

A flux-limited survey sees only the bright tail (left). The naive mean is badly biased; dividing the likelihood by the detection probability recovers the true population mean (right).

The one subtlety: Pdet(φ) is an integral over all data that would be detected, so it needs the selection function pdet(y) — usually estimated by injecting synthetic sources and measuring the recovery rate. Get that right and truncation is no obstacle; ignore it and every population parameter is wrong.

Interactive: selection bias and its correction

Drag the detection threshold. Only objects brighter than the cut are seen, so the naive mean of the detected sample (gold) drifts away from the truth. The selection-corrected posterior (blue) — dividing the likelihood by the detection probability — stays put.

Grey: full population (unobservable). Blue: detected (flux-limited) sample. Gold line: naive mean of the detected. Navy line: true mean. Blue curve: the selection-corrected posterior on μ.
Why astronomy leads here. Selection effects are unavoidable in survey science, so astronomers have developed the hierarchical selection formalism to a high art — it underpins gravitational-wave populations, exoplanet occurrence rates and luminosity functions alike.

Choosing the population distribution and its priors

The population model p(θ|φ) is the science: it encodes what you believe the distribution of the objects looks like. The choices matter, so make them deliberately.

Parametric populations

A Gaussian, a power law, a Schechter function, a truncated normal. Few hyperparameters, interpretable, but the shape is assumed. Good when theory suggests a form (an IMF slope, a mass function).

Flexible populations

Mixtures of Gaussians, splines, histograms (‘binned’ populations), or Gaussian-process rates. More parameters, fewer assumptions — used when the shape itself is the question (the black-hole mass spectrum).

Hyperpriors on variances — a real pitfall

The prior on the population scale τ needs care: too-broad “non-informative” priors (e.g. inverse-gamma with tiny parameters) can place huge mass near τ=0 and distort the answer when the number of groups is small. Weakly-informative choices — a half-Cauchy or half-normal on τ — are the modern recommendation (Gelman 2006).

τ ∼ Half-Normal(0, s)   or   Half-Cauchy(0, s) weakly-informative scale priors that behave well even with few groups
Prior sensitivity is a feature. Because the hierarchy makes assumptions explicit, you can (and should) test how much the conclusion depends on them — vary the population form and the hyperpriors and watch the posterior.

Sampling the posterior — and the geometry that fights back

Hierarchical posteriors are high-dimensional (every θi plus φ) and rarely have closed forms, so we sample. Gibbs sampling exploits conjugacy layer by layer; Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and its self-tuning variant NUTS (the engines of Stan, PyMC, NumPyro) use gradients to move efficiently in high dimensions.

The funnel

Hierarchies have a notorious pathology. When the population scale τ is small, the θi are squeezed into a narrow neck; when τ is large, they spread out. The joint posterior is a funnel, and a sampler tuned for the wide mouth stalls in the neck (and vice-versa).

Left: the centered parameterization’s funnel — the sampler must adapt across orders of magnitude in scale. Right: the non-centered reparameterization turns it into an easy, uniform Gaussian.

The cure is a change of variables. Instead of sampling θi directly (‘centered’), sample a standardized variable and rescale — the non-centered parameterization:

θi = μ + τ θ̃i,    θ̃i ∼ N(0, 1) decouples θ̃i from τ, flattening the funnel (Betancourt & Girolami 2015)

Interactive: watch a live sampler fight the funnel

Below, a Metropolis sampler explores Neal’s funnel in real time. In the centered parameterization it can reach the wide mouth but stalls at the neck — its fixed step is far too large down there, so almost every move is rejected and the deep neck is never explored. Switch to non-centered and the same target becomes a clean blob it samples effortlessly. Watch the acceptance rate.

Each dot is an accepted sample; the red dot is the current position. Centered: samples pile up in the mouth and the neck stays empty (low acceptance there). Non-centered: samples fill an easy Gaussian blob.
Practical rule. If your hierarchical sampler shows divergences or gets stuck at small τ, reparameterize non-centered first — it is the single most useful trick in applied HBM computation.

Beyond MCMC (I): variational inference

MCMC is asymptotically exact but can be too slow — a survey with millions of objects has millions of latent parameters, and every one needs sampling. Variational inference (VI) trades exactness for speed by turning inference into optimisation: pick a tractable family qλ(z) and find the member closest to the true posterior.

The evidence lower bound (ELBO), derived

Start from the log marginal likelihood and insert q. By Jensen’s inequality (log is concave):

log p(y) = log ∫ q(z)   p(y,z)/q(z)   dz  ≥  Eq[ log p(y,z) − log q(z) ] ≡ ELBO(q) the evidence lower bound: a tractable objective that never exceeds log p(y)

The gap is exactly a Kullback–Leibler divergence, which makes the goal precise:

log p(y) = ELBO(q) + DKL( q(z) ‖ p(z|y) ) since DKL ≥ 0, maximising the ELBO ⇐⇒ minimising the KL to the true posterior

Maximising the ELBO simultaneously pushes q toward the posterior and tightens a lower bound on the evidence (usable, with care, for model comparison).

Mean-field and coordinate ascent (CAVI)

The commonest family factorises the latent variables, q(z) = ∏j qj(zj). Maximising the ELBO over one factor with the rest fixed has a closed-form optimum:

log qj*(zj) = Eq−j[ log p(y, z) ] + const each factor ∝ the exponentiated expected log-joint under the other factors; cycling them raises the ELBO monotonically

Worked example: a Gaussian with unknown mean and precision

Data x1..N ∼ N(μ, τ−1), with priors μ|τ ∼ N(μ0, (λ0τ)−1) and τ ∼ Gamma(a0, b0). Take the mean-field q(μ)q(τ). The CAVI rule gives conjugate updates that you iterate to convergence:

q(μ) = N( μN, λN−1 ),   λN = (λ0+N) E[τ]  •  q(τ) = Gamma(aN, bN),   aN = a0 + N/2 bN = b0 + ½ Eμ[ Σ(xi−μ)² + λ0(μ−μ0)² ] — coupled through E[τ] and E[μ], E[μ²]

Each half is a standard distribution; the coupling (through E[τ] and E[μ²]) is what the iteration resolves. This is the textbook mean-field example, and the same recipe drives VI for full hierarchical models.

Black-box VI: the reparameterisation trick

For a differentiable model you need not derive updates by hand. Write a continuous latent as a deterministic transform of noise, z = gλ(ε) with ε ∼ N(0, I); then the ELBO gradient becomes a low-variance Monte-Carlo estimate:

∇λ ELBO = Eε[ ∇λ ( log p(y, gλ(ε)) − log qλ(gλ(ε)) ) ] autodiff through the simulator of q — the engine of ADVI (Stan), and of VI in Pyro / NumPyro

Richer families — normalizing-flow VI — replace the factorised Gaussian with an invertible neural transform, removing the mean-field independence error.

The catch. VI minimises DKL(q‖p), which is mode-seeking: it tends to underestimate posterior variance and can miss modes. Use it to screen large problems fast, then confirm the science-critical parameters with MCMC or nested sampling.

Beyond MCMC (II): nested sampling

When you need the evidence (to compare population models) or the posterior is multimodal, nested sampling is the workhorse — it computes Z and the posterior in a single run.

The key idea: integrate over prior volume

The evidence Z = ∫ L(θ) π(θ) dθ is a high-dimensional integral. Reparametrise it by the prior volume enclosed above a likelihood level:

X(λ) = ∫L(θ) > λ π(θ) dθ   →   Z = ∫01 L(X) dX X falls from 1 (all the prior) to 0 (the peak); the many-dimensional integral becomes a 1-D one

The algorithm

Keep N live points drawn from the prior. Repeat: identify the point of lowest likelihood Li, record it, and replace it with a fresh prior draw constrained to L > Li. The live set marches inward toward the peak, and the enclosed volume shrinks by a predictable statistical factor at each step:

Xi ≈ exp(− i / N) the largest of N uniforms on (0, X) shrinks the volume by E[log t] = −1/N per step

The estimators — evidence and posterior

The evidence is a weighted sum of the discarded (‘dead’) points, and those same points, reweighted, are the posterior:

Z ≈ ∑i Li wi,   wi = Xi−1 − Xi  •  posterior weight   pi = Li wi / Z one run yields the evidence and a set of weighted posterior samples together

The uncertainty is set by the information gained from prior to posterior, H = ∫ p(θ|y) log[p(θ|y)/π(θ)] dθ:

σ(log Z) ≈ √( H / N ) more live points N buy a proportionally more precise evidence

The hard sub-problem, and the tools

Everything hinges on efficiently drawing a new point from the prior subject to L > Li. The main libraries differ only in how they do this: MultiNest bounds the live points with ellipsoids; PolyChord and UltraNest use slice sampling (better in high dimension); dynesty offers both and dynamic nested sampling, which allocates live points to sharpen either the evidence or the posterior.

When to reach for it. Multimodal or strongly curved posteriors, and any time the evidence is the goal — “which population shape does the data prefer?”. See the companion evidence deck for the model-comparison side.

Beyond MCMC (III): simulation-based inference

Sometimes the per-object likelihood p(y|θ) has no formula at all — only a forward simulator y ∼ Sim(θ) exists (a full instrument, foregrounds and selection pipeline). Simulation-based inference (SBI / likelihood-free inference) learns a stand-in from simulations and plugs it into the hierarchy.

The classic route: approximate Bayesian computation (ABC)

Draw θ from the prior, simulate, and keep it only if the simulation resembles the data through a summary statistic s and a tolerance ε:

accept θ   if   ρ( s(ysim), s(yobs) ) < ε   →   samples → p(θ|y) as ε→0 simple and assumption-light, but it suffers badly with high-dimensional summaries and small ε

Neural SBI: three ways to learn the missing piece

NPE — posterior

Train a conditional density qφ(θ|y) (a normalizing flow) on {(θ, y)} drawn from prior + simulator, by minimising −E[log qφ(θ|y)]. Gives the posterior directly, and amortized.

NLE — likelihood

Learn a surrogate likelihood qφ(y|θ), then sample the posterior with ordinary MCMC using qφ·π.

NRE — the likelihood-ratio trick, derived

Train a classifier dφ(θ, y) to tell joint pairs (θ, y) ∼ p(θ, y) from marginal pairs (θ, y) ∼ p(θ)p(y). The Bayes-optimal classifier is d* = pjoint/(pjoint+pmarg), so the odds recover exactly the likelihood-to-evidence ratio:

r(θ, y) = d*/(1−d*) = p(θ,y) / [p(θ)p(y)] = p(y|θ) / p(y)  →  posterior ∝ r(θ,y) π(θ) a plain classifier yields the likelihood ratio — the basis of NRE and of ‘Evidence Networks’ (see the evidence deck)

Sequential variants (SNPE / SNLE / SNRE) retrain on simulations concentrated near the observed data, slashing the simulation budget for a single target.

The hierarchical inner integral, in practice (gravitational waves)

Even with tractable single-event likelihoods, the population step needs the per-event marginal likelihood under φ. It is estimated by importance sampling over that event’s posterior samples θs ∼ p(θ|di), obtained under a reference prior π0:

∫ L(di|θ) π(θ|φ) dθ  ≈  (Zi/S) ∑s π(θs|φ) / π0(θs) reweight stored single-event samples by the new population prior — no re-analysis of the raw data

The selection term is estimated the same way, from a large set of detected software injections drawn from πdraw:

Pdet(φ) = ∫ pdet(θ) π(θ|φ) dθ  ≈  (1/Ninj) ∑found π(θj|φ) / πdraw(θj) both Monte-Carlo sums are trustworthy only while the effective sample size stays large
ESS = ( ∑s ws )2 / ∑s ws2,   ws = π(θs|φ)/π0(θs) a low ESS silently biases the population posterior — the classic failure mode of GW population inference
Amortization pays off. An NPE/NRE estimator is trained once, then applied to every event or object almost instantly — decisive for catalogues of thousands. It connects back to the evidence deck’s neural estimators (learnt harmonic mean, Evidence Networks) for the model-comparison step.

Is the model any good — and which model?

Posterior predictive checks

Simulate replicated data from the fitted model and compare to the real data. If the model cannot reproduce salient features of what you saw, it is wrong — regardless of how tight the posterior looks. This is the first and most important diagnostic.

p(yrep | y) = ∫ p(yrep | φ)   p(φ | y)   dφ does data simulated from the posterior look like the real data?

Predictive comparison: LOO / WAIC

Leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) and the WAIC estimate out-of-sample predictive accuracy — ranking models by how well they predict new objects, penalising complexity automatically.

Evidence & Bayes factors

For discrete model choice (which population shape?), the marginal likelihood / Bayes factor is the coherent tool — the subject of the companion evidence deck.

Calibration & coverage

A well-specified hierarchy should be calibrated: its X% credible intervals should contain the truth X% of the time. Test this by simulation — the simulation-based calibration (SBC) check runs the whole pipeline on data drawn from the prior and verifies the ranks are uniform. Diagnostics like R̂ and effective sample size guard against non-convergence; divergences flag the funnel.

Discipline. Fit, check predictively, test calibration, compare models, report sensitivity to priors. A hierarchical posterior is only as trustworthy as the checks behind it.

The wider family of ideas — starting with the vocabulary

Before extending the hierarchy sideways into neighbouring methods, let us pin down the words that keep recurring. Each is simple once named.

Parameter vs hyperparameter

A parameter describes one object — a single star’s true brightness θi. A hyperparameter lives one level up: it describes the population the objects are drawn from — the mean μ and spread τ of all the brightnesses. “Hyper” just means “of the level above.”

Prior, hyperprior, marginal likelihood

A prior is your probability distribution for a quantity before its data. A hyperprior is a prior on a hyperparameter (a prior on μ, τ). The marginal likelihood is the probability of the data once the object parameters are averaged out — so it depends only on the hyperparameters.

Empirical Bayes: let the data set the prior

Empirical Bayes (EB) is a shortcut. Instead of putting a hyperprior on φ = (μ, τ) and integrating over it, you estimate φ directly from the data — by maximising the marginal likelihood — and then treat it as fixed. “Empirical” because the prior itself is learned from the data.

Worked toy model

Take n objects, each measured once with known noise σ:   yi ∼ N(θi, σ2), and a Gaussian population θi ∼ N(μ, τ2). Integrating out each latent θi (a Gaussian convolved with a Gaussian) gives the marginal distribution of the data in closed form:

yi ∼ N( μ,   σ2 + τ2 ) the observed scatter is the population spread τ2 plus the measurement noise σ2

Maximising this over μ and τ is now trivial — it is just fitting a single Gaussian to the yi:

μ̂ = ȳ = (1/n)Σ yi,    τ̂2 = max( 0,   sy2 − σ2 ),    sy2 = (1/n)Σ(yi − ȳ)2 the population spread is “the leftover scatter after removing what the noise explains”

Feed τ̂ back into the shrinkage rule from the partial-pooling page, θ̂i = (1−B)yi + Bμ̂ with B = σ2/(σ2+τ̂2), and the data have told you how much to pool:

  • if the objects scatter no more than their error bars (sy2 ≈ σ2) then τ̂2 ≈ 0 — they look identical, so pool them hard toward one common value;
  • if they scatter far more than the noise (sy2 ≫ σ2) then τ̂ is large — they are genuinely different, so barely pool.
What EB gets and what it misses. Empirical Bayes is fast and often excellent when there are many groups. Its one sin: it fixes φ at a single best value and forgets that φ itself is uncertain, so it is slightly overconfident when the groups are few. The full Bayesian hierarchy — a hyperprior on φ, integrated — is empirical Bayes done honestly.

Shrinkage is regularization

First the words. Overfitting is when a model chases noise in the data and then predicts new data poorly. Regularization is any penalty added to the fit that discourages extreme parameter values, to prevent exactly that. The MAP estimate (“maximum a posteriori”) is the parameter value at the peak of the posterior. A penalized likelihood maximises the log-likelihood minus a penalty — the frequentist twin of a MAP estimate.

The exact equivalence, worked

Fit a linear model y = Xw + noise, noise variance σ2, and put a Gaussian prior of width α on the weights, w ∼ N(0, α2I). The log-posterior is the log-likelihood plus the log-prior:

log p(w|y) = − ∥y − Xw∥2 / 2σ2  −  ∥w∥2 / 2α2  + const the second term — the Gaussian prior — is a penalty on large weights

Maximising it (the MAP) is identical to minimising a penalised least-squares with penalty strength λ = σ2/α2 — which is exactly ridge regression:

ŵ = argmin ∥y − Xw∥2 + λ∥w∥2 = ( XTX + λI )−1 XTy “add λ∥w∥2” (ridge) IS “put a Gaussian prior of width α on w”; the prior width sets λ

Swap the Gaussian prior for a Laplace (double-exponential) prior, p(w) ∝ e−|w|/b, and the penalty becomes λΣ|wj| — the LASSO, whose sharp peak at zero drives many weights exactly to zero (sparsity: a model that selects which features matter).

Gaussian prior ⇄ ridge (∥w∥2)  •  Laplace prior ⇄ LASSO (Σ|wj|, sparse) every ‘regulariser’ in machine learning is a prior in disguise

The hierarchical bonus

In plain ridge or LASSO you must tune λ by hand (usually cross-validation). In the hierarchy, λ = σ2/τ2 is fixed by the population scale τ — which the model learns from the data (empirical Bayes, previous page, or full Bayes). The hierarchy is regularization that chooses its own strength.

The frequentist echo: James–Stein

Shrinkage is not even a Bayesian idea at heart. Suppose you estimate a vector θ of p quantities from a single noisy draw y ∼ N(θ, I). The obvious estimate is θ̂ = y. Yet for p ≥ 3 the James–Stein estimator beats it — lower total expected squared error, for every true θ:

θ̂JS = ( 1 − (p−2)/∥y∥2 )   y it shrinks the raw estimate toward zero by a data-driven factor — the hierarchy’s shrinkage, with no prior at all

That a shrunk estimate can dominate the ‘obvious’ one, proven in 1961, is the frequentist confirmation that estimating quantities together beats estimating each alone — precisely what a hierarchical model does.

One mechanism, three vocabularies. Bayesians call it a population prior; machine learners call it regularization; classical statisticians call it James–Stein shrinkage. Same maths, and the hierarchy is the version that learns how much to shrink.

Gaussian processes, multilevel models, and cousins

Words first. A function-space prior is a probability distribution not over a few numbers but over whole functions. A Gaussian process (GP) is the workhorse example: a prior over functions such that the function’s values at any finite set of inputs are jointly Gaussian. It is pinned down by two choices: a mean function m(x) (usually 0) and a covariance function, or kernel, k(x, x′).

Kernel

k(x, x′) is the covariance between the function values f(x) and f(x′) — how strongly nearby points move together. It encodes what ‘smooth’ means for your problem.

Length scale & amplitude

The length scale ℓ is the input separation over which the function stays correlated — small ℓ = wiggly, large ℓ = smooth. The amplitude A is its typical vertical size. Both are hyperparameters.

Worked toy: GP regression

Take the squared-exponential kernel k(x,x′) = A2 exp[ −(x−x′)2 / 2ℓ2 ]. Given data (X, y) with noise σ2, the prediction at a new input x* is again Gaussian, with a mean and variance you can write down in closed form:

f̄(x*) = k*T ( K + σ2I )−1 y,    var(x*) = k(x*,x*) − k*T ( K + σ2I )−1 k* Kij = k(xi,xj),   (k*)i = k(x*,xi) — the GP interpolates, and its error bar grows away from the data

Where does the hierarchy hide? The kernel’s (A, ℓ) and the noise σ are hyperparameters: they set the distribution the function is drawn from. You learn them by maximising the marginal likelihood (empirical Bayes) or give them hyperpriors and integrate (full Bayes). A GP is thus an infinite-dimensional hierarchical prior — a population, but over functions instead of numbers. In astronomy GPs model stellar variability, instrument systematics, and transit / radial-velocity trends, sitting as one latent layer inside a larger hierarchy.

Stacking further: multilevel and non-parametric

Multilevel models

Populations within populations — stars within clusters within galaxies within cosmology. Each level adds its own hyperparameters; the layers stack as the science demands.

Dirichlet process (non-parametric)

A prior over distributions that lets the number of clusters grow with the data — for when you do not know how many components (stellar populations, source classes) there are.

The frequentist cousins, named

Random-effects and mixed models are the classical-statistics name for group-level parameters drawn from a distribution — a hierarchy in different clothing. Penalized likelihood is MAP estimation without the probabilistic story. All share the shrinkage mechanism; the Bayesian hierarchy generalises them by propagating every uncertainty and handling selection and measurement error in one framework.

One idea, many names. Empirical Bayes, ridge / LASSO, James–Stein, Gaussian processes, random effects, Dirichlet-process mixtures — all are hierarchies. Recognising this lets you borrow tools freely across statistics, machine learning and astronomy.

Hierarchical models across cosmology

Supernova cosmology

Type Ia SNe are standardisable, not standard: each has latent light-curve shape, colour and host-dust parameters drawn from populations, all fitted jointly with cosmology. Hierarchical analyses (BAHAMAS, Steve, and the BayeSN SED model) marginalise these nuisances coherently — and reveal how much the inferred dark energy depends on the dust model.

The distance ladder & H0

Cepheid period–luminosity relations have intrinsic scatter and metallicity terms; anchoring them to SNe is a multi-level regression. Hierarchical treatments of the ladder sit at the centre of the Hubble-tension debate, where every scatter term and outlier model matters.

Photometric redshifts

Each galaxy has a noisy redshift posterior; the survey’s redshift distribution n(z) is the population. Stacking individual estimates is biased — the correct n(z) comes from a hierarchy that infers the population while accounting for each galaxy’s uncertainty (Leistedt et al.).

Weak lensing & LSS

Bayesian hierarchical forward models infer shear and cosmological parameters while marginalising intrinsic galaxy shapes, photo-z errors and systematics as latent layers — the direction of travel for Rubin/LSST and Euclid analyses.

Common thread. The cosmological parameter you want sits atop layers of per-object nuisances and a hard selection function. The hierarchy is what lets you infer it without the nuisances biasing the answer.

The flagship: gravitational-wave populations

Modern gravitational-wave astronomy is hierarchical Bayesian inference at its most visible. Each detected merger yields a noisy posterior on its masses, spins and distance; the goal is the population — the mass spectrum, the spin distribution, the merger rate versus redshift — inferred from a few hundred such events, every one measured imprecisely and selected by the detectors’ sensitivity.

p(φ | {d}) ∝ p(φ) ∏i   [ ∫ L(di|θ) π(θ|φ) dθ ]  /  Pdet(φ) per-event marginal likelihood (over its parameter posterior) × selection correction — exactly the pages before, applied to black holes

Every ingredient of this deck appears at once: measurement error (each event’s posterior), the population model π(θ|φ) (a power law with a peak? a spin distribution?), selection effects Pdet (heavier, nearer binaries are easier to see), and model comparison (which mass model fits?). The per-event integral is done by importance-sampling over that event’s posterior samples.

What it has found

Structure in the black-hole mass spectrum (a peak near 35 M☉), the spin distribution, and the merger rate’s evolution with redshift — all population-level results from the LVK catalogues (GWTC-3 population analysis).

Why it’s the teaching example

Thrane & Talbot (2019) and Mandel, Farr & Gair (2019) made the hierarchical + selection formalism explicit and reproducible — the clearest modern write-ups of the whole machinery.

Interactive: infer the black-hole mass distribution

Detectors see heavy, nearby mergers more easily, so the observed masses are biased upward. Press Detect events to accumulate a catalogue and watch two curves build: the naive histogram of detected masses (biased high) and the selection-corrected reconstruction that divides out the detection probability — which converges to the true population, peak near 35 M☉ and all. More events, tighter reconstruction.

Dashed navy: true population p(m). Grey bars: detected masses (selection-biased). Blue: the selection-corrected hierarchical reconstruction. Higher selection strength = stronger high-mass bias to undo.
One model, all the pieces. If you understand GW population inference, you understand hierarchical Bayesian modelling with selection — it is this deck made concrete.

Stars, exoplanets and the Milky Way

Exoplanet occurrence rates

How many Earth-like planets per star? The catalogue is noisy and radically incomplete (small planets are hard to detect). Hierarchical inference with an explicit detection efficiency recovers the true occurrence-rate density — the Foreman-Mackey, Hogg & Morton (2014) framework — rather than the biased raw counts.

Gaia distances from parallax

A parallax is a noisy, sometimes negative, measurement; distance is latent. A hierarchical prior — a population model for where stars are in the Galaxy — regularises the inversion and gives sensible distances even for low-precision parallaxes (Bailer-Jones 2015, and Gaia distance catalogues).

Galaxy & stellar scaling relations

Tully–Fisher, mass–metallicity, the fundamental plane: relations with real intrinsic scatter, measured with errors in both variables. The hierarchical errors-in-variables fit (Kelly 2007) is the standard tool — and the reason quoted slopes are trustworthy.

Stellar populations & the IMF

Cluster ages, metallicity distributions, the initial mass function: each star is a noisy draw from a population. Hierarchical models infer the population parameters while propagating per-star uncertainties and selection.

Interactive: distance from a noisy parallax (Gaia)

A parallax ϖ is a noisy measurement; distance d is latent. Drag the parallax and its error. The naive 1/ϖ (gold) breaks down at low signal — and is meaningless for a negative parallax — but the hierarchical posterior (blue), likelihood × a Galactic distance prior, stays sensible (Bailer-Jones 2015).

Grey: the parallax likelihood mapped to distance. Green: the distance prior d²e−d/L (space density). Blue: the posterior (their product). Gold line: the naive 1/ϖ.
The pattern repeats. Occurrence rates, distances, scaling relations, mass functions — different sciences, one recipe: model the objects and their population together, correct for selection, propagate every error.

Software for hierarchical Bayesian modelling

Probabilistic programming

Stan (NUTS; the reference), PyMC, NumPyro (JAX, fast), and TensorFlow Probability. All support non-centered parameterizations and give you the funnel diagnostics automatically.

Samplers & diagnostics

emcee (affine-invariant ensemble), nested samplers dynesty / UltraNest / PolyChord (evidence too), and ArviZ + corner for diagnostics and plots (R̂, ESS, LOO, SBC).

Astronomy-specific

GWPopulation (GW population inference), BayeSN (hierarchical SN Ia SED), exoplanet (transit/RV with PyMC), linmix / LIRA (Kelly-style regression with scatter), and photo-z tools (chippr, PZFlow).

Simulation-based inference

sbi, swyft (truncated marginal neural ratio estimation), and normalizing-flow libraries (zuko, nflows) for likelihood-free hierarchies and amortized inference.

Getting started. For a first hierarchical model, write it in NumPyro or PyMC with a non-centered parameterization, check convergence in ArviZ, and validate with posterior predictive checks and SBC. Reach for nested sampling when you also need the evidence, and SBI when the likelihood is a simulator.

References & further reading

Textbooks and reviews first, then methods, then astronomy and cosmology applications. Links go to arXiv, the journal, or the code.

Textbooks, reviews & primers
A. Gelman, J. Carlin, H. Stern, D. Dunson, A. Vehtari & D. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed. (CRC, 2013) — the standard text; Ch. 5 on hierarchical models.
E. Thrane & C. Talbot, “An introduction to Bayesian inference in gravitational-wave astronomy: parameter estimation, model selection, and hierarchical models,” PASA 36, e010 (2019). arXiv:1809.02293 — the clearest modern primer.
D. W. Hogg, J. Bovy & D. Lang, “Data analysis recipes: Fitting a model to data,” (2010). arXiv:1008.4686.
M. Betancourt & M. Girolami, “Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Models,” (2015). arXiv:1312.0906 — the funnel & non-centered parameterization.
A. Gelman, “Prior distributions for variance parameters in hierarchical models,” Bayesian Analysis 1, 515 (2006).
Methods
B. C. Kelly, “Some Aspects of Measurement Error in Linear Regression of Astronomical Data,” ApJ 665, 1489 (2007). arXiv:0705.2774 — regression with errors & intrinsic scatter.
I. Mandel, W. Farr & J. Gair, “Extracting distribution parameters from multiple uncertain observations with selection biases,” MNRAS 486, 1086 (2019). arXiv:1809.02063 — the selection formalism.
D. Foreman-Mackey, D. W. Hogg, D. Lang & J. Goodman, “emcee: The MCMC Hammer,” PASP 125, 306 (2013). arXiv:1202.3665.
Applications in astronomy & cosmology
D. Foreman-Mackey, D. W. Hogg & T. Morton, “Exoplanet Population Inference and the Abundance of Earth Analogs from Noisy, Incomplete Catalogs,” ApJ 795, 64 (2014). arXiv:1406.3020.
C. A. L. Bailer-Jones, “Estimating Distances from Parallaxes,” PASP 127, 994 (2015). arXiv:1507.02105.
The LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA Collaboration, “The population of merging compact binaries inferred using gravitational waves through GWTC-3,” Phys. Rev. X 13, 011048 (2023). arXiv:2111.03634.
K. Mandel et al., “A hierarchical Bayesian SED model for Type Ia supernovae (BayeSN),” MNRAS (2022). arXiv:2008.07538.
B. Leistedt, D. Mortlock & H. Peiris, “Hierarchical Bayesian inference of galaxy redshift distributions from photometric surveys,” MNRAS (2016). arXiv:1602.05960.
